extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, theology, and early-modern church-state relations (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the principles Hobbes sets out about ecclesiastical power, excommunication, canon formation, and the relation of church authority to civil sovereignty in early-modern political theology. Useful for analysing norms about who may judge, pronounce sentence, make scripture law, and who is liable to ecclesiastical punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between judgment and pronouncing of sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment (determination of merit of a cause) belongs to the assembly of the faithful; pronouncing of sentence (the formal declaration) belongs to the Apostle or some Pastor as Prolocutor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes cites Matt. 18 and Paul (1 Cor. 5) to show assemblies hear causes and the Apostle/Pastor pronounces sentence; example: Paul pronounceth the Sentence though absent, while the assembly heard and condemned the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and origin of Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication (Aposunagogon Poiein) means to cast out of the synagogue — to remove from place of divine service — modeled on Jewish practice of separating those considered contagious in manners or doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes links the term to Jewish custom (e.g., separation of lepers) and frames excommunication as exclusion from public worship and congregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of excommunication when unsupported by civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: Without civil enforcement, excommunication's effect is social avoidance by the faithful (e.g., not eating with excommunicate persons) but not exclusion from public places by civil right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 1 Cor. 5 and Matt. 18: the faithful were to avoid excommunicate persons (no eating). Places remained open by civil commission; excommunication could not bar entry to synagogues unless owner/sovereign forbade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited worldly effect of excommunication upon apostates
rubrics_metrics.description: On Christians who apostatize in places where civil power persecutes or does not assist the church, excommunication has no worldly damage or terror; apostates return to favour of the world and are not worse off in the next world than non-believers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues excommunication without civil backing harms the Church more (provoking persecutors) than the excommunicated apostate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication affects only the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication has effect only on those who believe in Christ's coming and final judgment; it is a punishment sensible only to believers who expect exclusion from Christ's kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the penalty is exclusion from the kingdom of Christ, unbelievers or those who do not expect that judgment feel no punishment; thus it is a corrective for manners among the faithful, not an instrument to coerce opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for excommunication — moral offences, not mere doctrinal difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication lies for injustice and scandalous life (e.g., fornication, covetousness, idolatry, drunkenness, extortion), but Scripture shows no authority to excommunicate someone who holds the foundational belief 'Jesus was the Christ' merely for other doctrinal differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes discusses Titus 3:10 and 2 Tim. 2:23, interpreting 'reject/avoid foolish questions' as setting disputes aside, not excommunication; cites Peter and Paul not casting each other out despite controversy (Gal. 2.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on excommunicating heretics
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'haeretique' in Titus (one who teaches a private opinion forbidden by the Church) warrants rejection in the sense of ceasing to dispute, not necessarily ecclesiastical expulsion; admonition and giving over disputation is recommended rather than excommunication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes rejecting (paraitou/avoid) from formal excommunication and warns against making new articles of faith that burden conscience and break church union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for a person to be liable to excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: A person must be a member of some lawful assembly/church that has power to judge the cause; where no community or judicial power exists, there can be no excommunication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this follows that one church cannot excommunicate another (either equal power → would be schism, or subordinate → effectively same church), and excommunication presupposes an assembly's jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineffectiveness of excommunication against sovereigns and within sovereign dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication of a sovereign prince or assembly has no practical effect: subjects are bound by natural law to attend their sovereign and cannot lawfully expel or refuse to eat with their sovereign; excommunication cannot lawfully separate kings and states beyond normal policy effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues political obligations to one's sovereign override ecclesiastical sanctions; excommunication may only instigate political conflict but not enforce social avoidance of sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication does not harm true, unfeigned Christians in this world
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Christian (who believes Jesus is the Christ and has the Spirit of God dwelling in him) cannot receive harm from human excommunication; only hypocrites whose manners betray their profession are liable to ecclesiastical censure insofar as their actions violate civil law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes grounds this in 1 John texts: those with the Spirit are not subject to harm by men; external actions are what the Church can judge, and those actions are unlawful only when against the commonwealth's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to practical familial and domestic effects of excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parent or master is excommunicate, their children or servants are not forbidden to keep company or eat with them; extension of excommunication to dependents would cause undue hardship and contravene filial/marital duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes practical considerations: forbidding eating with excommunicated parents would often deprive children of sustenance and contravene apostolic precepts to obey parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of ecclesiastical power — teaching and direction, not coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of excommunication and other ecclesiastical functions is limited to the end for which Apostles and pastors were commissioned: teaching and guiding men toward salvation (the next world), not ruling by coercive commands in this world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes compares teachers abandoning obstinate scholars to pastors abandoning disobedient disciples; ecclesiastical authority is pedagogical rather than sovereign coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter of Scripture — no universal apostolic interpretive authority pre-civil sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Before Christian civil sovereigns, apostles and preachers persuaded by reason and testimony; those they addressed judged the force of scriptural proof themselves — no one apostle had a legally binding interpretive authority over converts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses Paul's preaching in Thessalonica: citing Scripture makes the hearer judge the meaning; converts accepted writings by faith, not because apostles had sovereign interpretive power; only when pastors/sovereigns could authorise interpreters would that change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between canonicity as rule and as law — civil sovereigns make Scripture obligatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A writing may be canonical (a rule) as moral or doctrinal guidance, but becomes law (obligatory) only when the civil sovereign, to whom people have submitted authority, makes it so; private acceptance by converts does not make Scripture legally binding on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes internal faith (invisible, exempt from human jurisdiction) from outward actions (subject to civil law); he asserts New Testament becomes law only where lawful civil power commands obedience to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten Commandments as law via civil sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Ten Commandments were given by God, their obligatory force as law to Israel derived from Moses (who, with the High Priests, functioned as civil sovereign) and the people's covenant to obey him; civil sovereigns made scripture binding in civil polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes breaks the Decalogue into the first table (law of sovereignty) and second table (duty between men) and shows canonization depends on the civil institutional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and Levitical laws as civil laws delivered by Moses
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial (magistrates' rules) and Levitical (rites/ceremonies) laws were given by Moses to Israel's magistrates and priests and thus became positive laws by virtue of his civil sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats these laws as examples of scripture becoming law through a recognized civil sovereign (Moses/Aaron/high priests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old and New Testaments became canonical/lawful by civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old Testament became law for Israel at the restoration under Esdras (a civil/high-priestly authority); the New Testament became canonical in practice among Christians through the writings and reverence of early Fathers but only became obligatory law where civil sovereigns made it so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes traces canon formation to political authority (translation into Greek under Ptolemy's library, Esdras, councils) and maintains that councils or fathers absent civil sovereign authority cannot make binding laws for all Christians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils' decrees are counsel not universal laws without civil sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of councils (including Apostolic councils) may lay burdens or conditions for converts but are not universal laws enforceable on all Christians unless issued with the authority of civil sovereigns; councils instruct pastors what to teach but cannot legislate for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes reads Acts 15's formula ('It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us...') as counsel; councils set conditions for those accepting Christianity but do not create civil obligations absent sovereign legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical officers in apostolic times — magisterial vs ministerial offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Magisterial offices (preaching, sacraments, teaching) include apostles and pastors ordained by Christ; ministerial offices (deacons) handle secular necessities of the church. Apostles were distinguished by being witnesses of Christ's resurrection (martyr-witness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes delineates the functional division and a qualification for apostleship (seeing Christ after resurrection or conversing with him before), illustrating limits of ecclesiastical institutional authority in early church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits on canonical enforcement of reading/teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Early canons forbidding public reading of books other than those in the churches (e.g., Laodicea Can. 59) were addressed to ecclesiastics (those authorized to read publicly) and thus did not ipso facto bind every Christian privately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes the distinction between mandates directed at ecclesiastical office-holders and obligations assumed by the laity; canonical prohibitions often regulated public worship and clergy, not private belief.
